record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps model complexity and evaluates out-of-sample performance for neural networks, random forests, and linear models, using settings and comparisons different from the original double-descent studies.
record.gate_note: The paper directly examines double descent in a neural network and contrasts it with random forests and linear regression. Figure 3 values are shown only graphically; the text describes a neural-network revival and says random-forest test performance remains constant as training fit rises. Figure 2 also reports a complexity sweep for OLS and Greedy LS. The cited findings from other papers are not recorded as rows. Results in Figures 4 and 6 concern implicit pruning of CART, Boosting, and MARS ensembles; those comparisons do not establish whether test error has a peak at the interpolation threshold, so they are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper sweeps capacity for a neural network, random forest and OLS (Figures 2–3). Its central double-descent argument (Section 3.2) is that Belkin et al.'s random-forest double descent is an artifact of counting trees as capacity. With tree depth as capacity, it reports a single monotonic descent instead. This is a specific argument, backed by results, that V4 needs restating for RF, so T5 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that the authors argue double descent reported for RF by Belkin et al. is an artifact of defining capacity as tree count past interpolation. They also say OLS shows a double-descent renaissance but still gains greatly from tuning. Their main thesis is that bagging and perturbing greedy learners performs implicit optimal early stopping.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses its own simulations and complexity sweeps rather than reproducing the original double-descent experiments; it compares neural networks, RF, and OLS under its stated settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper distinguishes results by model class and complexity measure: neural-network layers, RF minimum node size/tree depth, and number of regressors for OLS. Figure 3 discusses a high-noise setting; Figure 2 uses SNR=2.

fits_no_version.finding: Section 3.2 argues that Belkin et al.'s RF double descent comes from treating the number of trees as capacity. More trees act as ensembling regularization (law of large numbers), not added function capacity. With depth as capacity, RF shows a monotonic descent, not a U-shape.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent double descent in tree ensembles reflects a capacity axis mixing complexity with averaging; on a pure capacity axis the curve is monotonic rather than U-shaped.

record.problems: The Figure 2 and Figure 3 values are available only in plots, with no exact numerical values stated in the text. The text does not locate the neural-network peak relative to interpolation. The Figure 3 description of RF performance is qualitative.
record.rows_left_out: Figures 4 and 6 report complexity sweeps for CART, Boosting, and MARS under multiple DGPs and noise levels, including plain and randomized ensembles. They are omitted because the reported outcome concerns implicit pruning and performance relative to an ex-post stopping point, not test error peaking at the interpolation threshold.

untested.parts: Location of the peak relative to the size that just fits the training set; width sweeps; exact test-error values.
Whether RF shows a second descent on Belkin et al.'s own capacity axis (the paper argues against that axis rather than re-running it); model classes beyond NN, RF, OLS and Greedy LS.
Noise level is varied but not linked to peak size; regularization tuning versus the peak is not tested.
No effective parameter count is measured or replotted against.

missing.what: Figure 3 low-noise / other-environment panels for NN and RF. The text says NN depth needs tuning 'in each environment' while the deepest RF is always best.

record.verdict_notes: Belkin et al. (1812.11118) is an original source, but this study is not, so verdicts apply. All curve values are figure-only, so the states rest on the authors' verbal descriptions.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not state that the neural-network peak occurs near the size at which the training set is just fit; exact curve values are not stated in the text.
Test error over training epochs is not swept.
Training-sample size is not varied near an interpolation threshold to test whether more data raises test error.
The evidence is limited to the particular model classes and settings reported; it does not establish a general curve across model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across axes.
The paper varies noise in other simulation results, but does not test whether double-descent peaks are driven by noise, split into multiple peaks, or disappear under optimally tuned regularization.

The paper argues that a random-forest capacity definition used in cited work is misleading, but does not measure an effective parameter count or show that replotting against it yields an ordinary U-shaped curve.
